entries.proposition: Design: a secondary analysis of a retrospective single-centre cohort of 142 neonates with HIE and cooling, transfusion exposure over the whole stay.
entries.snippet: This study is a secondary analysis of a previously described retrospective cohort of neonates with HIE undergoing TH at a single tertiary-level Neonatal Intensive Care Unit with a distinct primary objective focused on transfusion burden and factors associated with transfusion exposure.

experimental_context.system: human neonates with hypoxic-ischemic encephalopathy treated with therapeutic hypothermia, single tertiary NICU, retrospective cohort 2014-2022 (n = 142)

entries.proposition: Unit thresholds: red cells below 10 g/dL (11 if respiratory support); plasma if PT-INR above 2, or 1.50-1.99 with low fibrinogen; prothrombin complex concentrate if INR 1.50-1.99 with normal fibrinogen.
entries.snippet: We administered fresh frozen plasma (FFP) in patients with prothrombin time expressed as International normalized ratio (PT-INR) > 2.

entries.proposition: Clinical discretion applied to borderline cases and any clinically visible bleeding.
entries.snippet: Clinical discretion was possible for all borderline cases or those with any clinically visible bleeding (such as pulmonary bleeding, hematuria, umbilical bleeding, nasal bleeding, gastric bleeding, or petechiae).

entries.proposition: Result: 74 of 142 infants (52.1 percent) received at least one product, 215 episodes, median 2.
entries.snippet: Overall, 74 (52.1%) infants received at least one blood component or coagulation product during hospital stay, whereas 68 (47.9%) did not receive any transfusion.

entries.snippet: During hospital stay, 48/142 (33.8%) infants were exposed to a single blood component or coagulation product, and 26/142 (18.3%) received two or more different blood components or coagulation products.

entries.proposition: Independent associations with any transfusion: visible bleeding aOR 12.95 (1.34-124.97, 16 infants with bleeding) and respiratory support aOR 2.98; acidosis, lactate, seizures not significant after adjustment.
entries.snippet: In multivariable logistic regression analysis, clinically visible bleeding (aOR 12.95, 95% CI 1.34–124.97; p = 0.027) and need for respiratory support (aOR 2.98, 95% CI 1.19–7.45; p = 0.020) remained independently associated with transfusion exposure

entries.proposition: Text: intracranial bleeding and hypoxic-ischaemic injury on MRI were more frequent among transfused infants.
entries.snippet: Notably, intracranial bleeding and hypoxic–ischemic injury on brain MRI were more frequently observed among infants who received transfusions, likely reflecting a higher underlying disease severity, whereas a normal MRI was more common in non-transfused infants (Table 4).

entries.proposition: The MRI comparison is unadjusted and the authors say it should not be read as causal; transfusion exposure is called a proxy for disease severity.
entries.snippet: In particular, the comparison of pathological brain MRI findings between transfused and not-transfused infants was unadjusted, and the higher frequency of pathological MRI findings among transfused infants likely reflects confounding by underlying disease severity rather than a direct effect of transfusion on neurological injury; this association should not be interpreted as causal.

entries.snippet: Fourth, the number of infants with clinically visible bleeding and specific bleeding subtypes was relatively small, resulting in wide confidence intervals for some effect estimates.

entries.proposition: The Discussion lists transfusion harms (circulatory overload, immunomodulation, allergic or febrile reactions, infection) and states that transfusion stimulates inflammation, cytokine release and endothelial activation (cited).
entries.snippet: Blood products are administered to improve oxygen delivery and support hemodynamics, but transfusions also stimulate systemic inflammation, pro-inflammatory cytokine release, and endothelial activation, which have been implicated in adverse outcomes in critically ill neonates [15,16].
